title: Cicada Emergence Map: Which Brood, Which Year
description: Find the periodical cicada brood covering a US location with the Cicada Emergence Map — brood ranges and next emergence years by 13/17-year cycle. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, central Illinois sits in Brood XIII's recorded range — a 17-year brood that emerged in 2024 and is next due in 2041 — while Kentucky's Brood XIV, out in 2025, returns in 2042.
quick_answer: The Cicada Emergence Map identifies which periodical cicada brood's recorded range covers a US location, and computes that brood's next emergence year from its 13- or 17-year cycle. Set the location and read the brood — Magicicada's extraordinary calendar, mapped.
steps_intro: Underground for 13 or 17 years, then a few loud weeks. Whose ground are you on?

body.t: Weddings, graduations and open houses in brood country check the year first — a 2041 Illinois June will be loud, and the map says which counties carry the chorus.

for the other great American garden map.
Brood maps are refined by public reports each emergence. Knowing your brood's name and year is the citizen scientist's first credential.

13 and 17 are primes — cycles that rarely sync with predators or with each other. The 2024 co-emergence of Broods XIII and XIX was the first since 1803; this map's arithmetic shows why such overlaps are centuries apart.

Brood XIII (17-year, Illinois-centred) and Brood XIX (13-year, southeastern) emerged together in 2024 — an overlap last seen in 1803 and next due 221 years later: the cycles' least common multiple is 221 years, and geography must also cooperate.

examples.label: Example · Brood X, the famous one

body.t: Brood X — the 'Great Eastern Brood' around Washington, DC and the mid-Atlantic — filled 2021's headlines and returns in 2038 (2021 + 17). If a location's brood is X, its calendar is already set.

popular_table.title: Notable broods and their calendars
popular_table.intro: From published brood records (USDA Forest Service and university entomology) — last emergence plus period gives the next.
popular_table.note: Broods are numbered with Roman numerals by entomologists. Ranges here are the recorded brood ranges; stragglers a year early or late (especially 4-year-early 'shadow' emergences) are a documented Magicicada habit, not a map error.

faq: Soil temperature — nymphs emerge when soil at about 20 cm depth reaches roughly 18°C (64°F), usually after rain. The year is the brood's clockwork; the week is spring's.
Fifteen recognised broods in the eastern US: twelve on 17-year cycles and three on 13-year cycles, numbered I–XXX with gaps where broods have gone extinct or were never assigned.
No — locusts are grasshoppers. 'Seventeen-year locust' is a settler-era misnomer stuck to a true cicada (genus Magicicada), harmless to people and pets.

Egg-laying slits flag small branches ('flagging') and can set back young or stressed trees; established trees shrug it off. The underground years of root feeding are gentle. Netting protects saplings in emergence springs.
Those appear every summer in small numbers and are not broods — this map covers periodical Magicicada only; a lone August singer is a different insect entirely.
Range edges are lived gradients, not fences — a few miles can change which brood sings loudest. The map gives the recorded range for the point; both broods may visit the borderland.
